entities.description: A system where people in different locations are connected and see each other/things on a screen in real-time.

entities.name: SCREEN
entities.description: A display device used to view content, which aids interaction in a video conferencing system but does not create a virtual environment.

entities.name: VIRTUAL ENVIRONMENT
entities.description: The first characteristic of a VR system where the user is surrounded by a computer-generated environment.

entities.name: REAL TIME
entities.description: The state of events happening immediately as they occur, which distinguishes video conferencing from a virtual environment.

entities.name: REAL WORLD ENVIRONMENT
entities.description: An environment that is physically real but viewed through a medium like a screen.

entities.name: IMMERSIVE EXPERIENCE
entities.description: The second characteristic of a VR system involving the blocking of senses to feel present in a virtual world.

entities.name: INTERACTIVE
entities.description: The third characteristic of a VR system where the user is able to change or influence what is being displayed.

entities.name: VR SYSTEM
entities.description: A system characterized by three main requirements: a virtual environment, an immersive experience, and interactivity.

entities.name: 3D MOVIE
entities.description: A popular form of cinema where users wear glasses to see content in 3D, providing a virtual environment and semi-immersive experience.

entities.name: 3D GLASS
entities.description: A wearable device used by viewers to perceive 3D content in a movie.

entities.name: AUDITORIUM
entities.description: A physical location where people sit to watch a 3D movie.

entities.name: SEMI-IMMERSIVE
entities.description: A level of immersion that is partly achieved by blocking visual and auditory senses, as seen in 3D movies.

relationships.description: The system uses a screen to display the connection to other people.
The system functions in real time, which prevents it from being considered a virtual environment.
Virtual environment is the first required characteristic of a VR system.
Immersive experience is the second required characteristic of a VR system.
Interactivity is the third required characteristic of a VR system.
Users wear 3D glasses to watch a 3D movie.
A 3D movie provides a virtual environment to the viewer.
A 3D movie provides a semi-immersive experience because it partially blocks senses.
A 3D movie is identified as not being interactive because the user cannot change what is displayed.

entities.description: A phenomenon related to usability and acceptability in VR, characterized by three aspects: causes, evaluation, and mitigation.

entities.name: INTERNAL FACTORS
entities.description: A set of individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can contribute to an increased likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness.

entities.name: EXTERNAL FACTORS
entities.description: Factors external to the user that can cause cyber sickness, including hardware and VR content.

entities.name: HARDWARE
entities.description: A sub-factor of external factors that can cause cyber sickness.

entities.name: VR CONTENT
entities.description: A sub-factor of external factors that can cause cyber sickness; it can be categorized as general VR content or controllable content.

entities.name: AGE
entities.description: An internal factor where children (2-12 years) may exhibit increased sensitivity to cyber sickness, while older persons may experience higher levels; the relationship is more visible in controllable content.

entities.name: GENDER
entities.description: An internal factor whose impact on cyber sickness has been studied with inconclusive results, with some studies suggesting women may experience more severe cases.

entities.name: HEAD-MOUNTED DISPLAYS, HMDS
entities.description: A hardware device that, when used by females, is associated with an increase in cyber sickness.

Gender is cited as another internal factor contributing to cyber sickness.
Studies indicate a relationship between age and cyber sickness susceptibility.

Usage of HMDs by females is associated with an increase in cyber sickness.
The relationship between age and cyber sickness is more visible when viewing controllable content versus general VR content.

entities.description: The visual experience of perceiving depth, which is facilitated by the inter-pupillary distance and provided by VR displays.

entities.name: CYBERSICKNESS
entities.description: Also referred to as visually induced motion sickness (CS), it is a condition where users experience symptoms related to virtual reality usage, influenced by internal and external factors.

entities.name: PRIOR EXPOSURE
entities.description: One of the conditions that can satisfy a positive correlation regarding the onset of cybersickness.

entities.name: REPEATED EXPOSURE
entities.description: One of the conditions that can satisfy a positive correlation regarding the onset of cybersickness.

entities.name: PHYSICAL CONDITIONS
entities.description: An internal factor responsible for the induction or severity of cybersickness.

entities.name: BODY AWARENESS
entities.description: A specific physical condition defined as the ability of the user to attend to and perceive bodily sensations, which is an internal factor for CS.

entities.name: POOR SLEEP QUALITY
entities.description: A factor that may lead to, contribute to, or increase the severity of cybersickness.

entities.name: RETINAL ECCENTRICITY
entities.description: A physical attribute where people with greater retinal eccentricity may be more susceptible to cybersickness.

entities.name: MULTIPLE SCLEROSIS
entities.description: A neurological condition that may cause individuals to experience more severe cybersickness symptoms.

entities.name: PHYSICAL POSITION
entities.description: An internal factor where the posture of the user (e.g., standing vs. sitting) impacts susceptibility to and the onset of cybersickness.

entities.name: EMOTIONAL CONDITIONS
entities.description: Internal factors including emotions at the time of usage that affect the likelihood of experiencing cybersickness.

entities.name: NEGATIVE EMOTIONS
entities.description: Includes anxiety, stress, and frustration; these are typically associated with an increased likelihood of experiencing cybersickness.

entities.name: NEUROTICISM
entities.description: A personality trait that may increase the likelihood of experiencing cybersickness.

entities.name: AGE
entities.description: An internal factor related to the user's susceptibility to cybersickness.

entities.name: GENDER
entities.description: An internal factor related to the user's susceptibility to cybersickness.

entities.name: MOTION SICKNESS SUSCEPTIBILITY
entities.description: An internal factor regarding a user's inherent tendency to experience motion sickness.

entities.name: HARDWARE
entities.description: An external factor category that was initially thought to be the primary cause of cybersickness but is now seen as less fundamental than other aspects of devices.

entities.name: TECHNOLOGY
entities.description: The advancement of technology was once thought to eliminate cybersickness, but many problems remain despite technological progress.

entities.name: DEVICES
entities.description: Specific aspects of devices, regardless of how advanced they are, are responsible for inducing cybersickness.

entities.name: DISPLAY RESOLUTION
entities.description: A factor of devices where higher resolution leads to a better experience and reduced cybersickness up to a certain point.

entities.name: CYBERSICKNESS
entities.description: A physical discomfort or disorientation experienced by users in virtual environments, also referred to as CS.

entities.name: RESOLUTION
entities.description: A measure of image clarity in a virtual environment, where changes from 1K to 2K affect CS induction, but changes beyond 2K have little effect.

entities.name: LATENCY
entities.description: The time delay between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.

entities.name: LATENCY JITTER
entities.description: The variability or inconsistency in latency, where the time gap between physical actions and virtual reflections keeps on varying.

entities.name: HMD
entities.description: Head-mounted display, a hardware component used for semi-immersive VR experiences that can induce more cyber sickness compared to conventional monitors.

entities.name: CONVENTIONAL MONITORS
entities.description: Standard display devices used for non-immersive VR systems.

entities.name: TYPE OF DISPLAY
entities.description: A hardware factor including various screens and headsets that influences the severity of CS symptoms.

entities.name: STEREOSCOPIC 3D VIDEOS
entities.description: A type of video content used to compare experiences across different projection devices.

entities.name: FLAT SCREENS
entities.description: A type of projection device used for displaying stereoscopic 3D videos.

entities.name: PANORAMIC SCREENS
entities.description: A type of projection device used for displaying stereoscopic 3D videos.

entities.name: VR HEADSETS
entities.description: Hardware used to experience stereoscopic 3D videos, found to cause more CS than flat or panoramic screens.

entities.name: CYBERSICKNESS
entities.description: A form of discomfort and disorientation caused by virtual reality, which can be induced by longer exposure to turbulent motions, sensory mismatches, and specific locomotion factors.

entities.name: ANGULAR VELOCITY
entities.description: A measure of rotational speed; cyber sickness increases as angular velocity increases, especially around the x and y axes.

entities.name: VISUAL MOTION
entities.description: Movement perceived by the user in a virtual environment, which is linked to the occurrence of cyber sickness.

entities.name: LOCOMOTION
entities.description: The means of moving within a virtual world, encompassing how users move and how scenes transition.

entities.name: SENSORY MISMATCH
entities.description: An occurrence where users' virtual movements do not match their physical movements, resulting in discomfort and disorientation leading to cyber sickness.

entities.name: CONTROL OVER MOTION
entities.description: The degree and manner in which a user controls their movement in a virtual environment, affecting presence and cyber sickness.

entities.name: PRESENCE
entities.description: The sense of being in a virtual reality; it has a direct relationship with control over motion and an indirect relationship with cyber sickness.

entities.name: HAND-BASED MOTION CONTROL
entities.description: A type of control mechanism that leads to significantly less cyber sickness compared to whole-body motion control.

entities.name: WHOLE-BODY MOTION CONTROL
entities.description: A type of control mechanism that leads to more cyber sickness compared to hand-based motion control.

entities.name: TRANSITION
entities.description: The way scenes change and movement occurs from one field of view to another.

entities.name: TELEPORTATION
entities.description: An instantaneous transition method found to be less cyber-sickness-inducing compared to naturalistic free movement.

entities.name: NATURALISTIC FREE MOVEMENT
entities.description: Movement types such as walking, running, and jumping, which are found to be more cyber-sickness-inducing than teleportation.

entities.name: FIELD OF VIEW
entities.description: The extent to which the user's field of vision is captured by the display in a VR headset; it affects immersion and cyber sickness susceptibility.

entities.name: IMMERSION
entities.description: The sense of being absorbed in the virtual environment; it is increased by a larger field of view and decreased by an excessively narrow field of view.

entities.name: HEAD MOVEMENT
entities.description: The physical movement of the head to look for things in an environment; increased head movement due to a narrow field of view can exacerbate cyber sickness.

relationships.description: Cyber sickness increases with the increase in angular velocity.
A sensory mismatch results in discomfort and disorientation which leads to cyber sickness.
Control over motion has a direct effect on presence (more control means greater presence).
Control over motion has an indirect effect on cyber sickness through presence.
A greater sense of presence in virtual reality can lead to a lower likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness.
Hand-based motion control leads to significantly less cyber sickness.

entities.name: FOV ADJUSTMENT
entities.description: A category of strategies and techniques used by developers to adjust the Field of View (FOV) to improve user experience and reduce the chances of cybersickness.

entities.name: SYMMETRIC MASK
entities.description: A classical FOV adjustment technique where the periphery is occluded in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity; it can affect presence.

entities.name: ASYMMETRIC MASK
entities.description: An FOV adjustment technique that obscures the periphery with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible; also considered an adaptive restrictor.

entities.name: SIDE RESTRICTOR
entities.description: A specific type of asymmetric mask that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn.

entities.name: GROUND VISIBLE RESTRICTOR
entities.description: An FOV adjustment technique where the ground plane remains visible during movement.

entities.name: DYNAMIC VISUAL BLUR
entities.description: A technique to reduce the possibility of cybersickness by obscuring or reducing the clarity of certain visual regions.

entities.name: DEPTH OF FIELD BLUR
entities.description: A type of dynamic visual blur that makes use of well-known depth cues in human vision.

entities.name: PERIPHERAL BLUR
entities.description: A type of dynamic visual blur that involves dynamic non-salient region blurring.

entities.name: REST FRAMES
entities.description: Fixed elements within the virtual environment that remain stationary relative to the real world regardless of the user's movements, used to reduce cybersickness.

entities.name: INDEPENDENT VISUAL BACKGROUNDS
entities.description: Rest frames attached to the head reference frame, such as clouds, grids, and a virtual nose, which remain stationary relative to the user's movement.

entities.name: OPTICAL FLOW MANIPULATION
entities.description: A technique referring to visually mixing optical flow patterns that are in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion.

entities.name: GEOMETRICAL SIMPLIFICATION
entities.description: A technique used to reduce perceived optical flow by simplifying the geometry of the virtual environment.

entities.description: A sophisticated piece of equipment and a common metaphor for VR that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components to place images directly in front of a user's eyes using one or two screens.

entities.name: MONOSCOPIC VIEWING
entities.description: Viewing provided by an HMD when it is using only one small screen.

entities.name: STEREOSCOPIC VIEWING
entities.description: Viewing provided by an HMD when it is using two small screens; it is more common than monoscopic viewing.

entities.name: NON-SEE-THROUGH HMD
entities.description: A category of HMD typically used in VR where the user's view of the outside world is blocked.

entities.name: OPTICAL SEE-THROUGH HMD
entities.description: A category of HMD typically used in AR where the user sees the real world through the device.

entities.name: VIDEO SEE-THROUGH HMD
entities.description: A category of HMD typically used in augmented virtuality that supports experiencing an artificial environment with real-world images.

entities.name: AUGMENTED VIRTUALITY
entities.description: An experience of an artificial or virtual environment within which some real-world images or videos appear on a real-time basis.

entities.name: WORLD FIXED DISPLAY
entities.description: A category of display that renders graphics onto surfaces that do not move with the head.

entities.name: CAVE
entities.description: A display that completely surrounds the user, representing an extreme of world-fixed displays.

entities.name: FISH TANK DISPLAY
entities.description: An early example of a world-fixed display for VR developed in 1993, showing a stereo image of a 3D scene on a fixed monitor.

entities.name: TRACKER
entities.description: An input part used to track the head position of the observer in a world-fixed display setup.

entities.name: HAPTIC DEVICES
entities.description: An input part used in the world-fixed display setup to provide tactile feedback.

relationships.description: HMDs use one screen to provide this type of viewing.

entities.name: ALIGNMENT

entities.name: FIDUCIAL MARKERS
entities.description: Reflectors or tags used to significantly aid in the registration process between real and virtual worlds.

entities.name: COMPUTER VISION
entities.description: Techniques used to perform registration even in the absence of fiducial markers.

entities.name: INTEGRATION
entities.description: The third stage of tracking where sensory output data streams arriving at regular sampling intervals are processed.

entities.name: SAMPLING INTERVAL
entities.description: Represented as delta t, it is the discrete interval at which the sensor data stream arrives.

entities.name: PERCEPTUAL DESIGN
entities.description: A design area related to the output of an XR system, intended to be designed alongside interaction design to create the best possible illusion of reality.

entities.name: PRESENCE
entities.description: The primary goal of an XR system, which is to give the user a sense of reality as if they are in the real world, achieved through an illusion of reality.

entities.name: ILLUSION OF REALITY
entities.description: The state created by designing interaction and perceptual stimuli so that the user perceives the virtual environment as their regular, familiar system.

entities.name: XR
entities.description: Extended Reality, which includes VR, AR, and MR systems, where the goal is to create a better experience through the illusion of reality.

entities.name: VR
entities.description: Virtual Reality systems where users are supposed to be totally immersed in a virtual environment, requiring a high degree of illusion of reality and presence.

entities.name: AR
entities.description: Augmented Reality systems where immersion is partial because the user can still view or experience the real world.

entities.name: MR
entities.description: Mixed Reality systems where immersion is partial because the user can still view or experience the real world.

entities.name: IMMERSION
entities.description: The feeling of being totally immersed in a virtual environment; it is achieved when the system successfully fools the user's perception into believing they are in a different world.

entities.name: PERCEPTION
entities.description: The process by which our senses and physiology work to interpret the environment; the system aims to "fool" this process to create presence.

entities.name: PERCEPTUAL SYSTEM

entities.name: PERCEPTUAL PSYCHOLOGY
entities.description: The science of understanding how the brain converts sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena, providing guidelines for building better hardware and understanding system effects on the user

entities.name: EXTENDED REALITY SYSTEMS
entities.description: Interactive systems where the goal is to explicitly extend the idea of reality, which is deeply embedded in human psychology

entities.name: SENSORY STIMULATION
entities.description: Signals from the real world that come to sensors and are converted by the brain into perceived phenomena

entities.name: PERCEIVED PHENOMENA
entities.description: The results of the brain converting sensory stimulation into internal experiences

entities.name: PRESENCE
entities.description: A state or feeling of being in a virtual environment, for which perceptual psychology can provide clues

entities.name: HARDWARE
entities.description: The physical components of a system, for which perceptual psychology provides guidelines for improvement

entities.name: VIRTUAL WORLD
entities.description: A simulated environment where questions regarding object distance, resolution, and user height are addressed

entities.name: VIRTUAL OBJECT
entities.description: A simulated item within a virtual world, where resolution needs to be high enough to avoid seeing pixels

entities.name: NAUSEATED
entities.description: A physical sensation of sickness that can be experienced by a user interacting with a system

entities.name: TIREDNESS
entities.description: A tiring effect that can vary between different experiences with a system

entities.name: SENSE ORGANS
entities.description: The biological components of the human body used to capture signals from the environment

entities.name: NEURAL PATHWAYS
entities.description: The biological connections between sense organs and the brain

entities.name: VIDEO RESOLUTION
entities.description: The amount of detail in a virtual display, used to determine if pixels are visible to the user

entities.name: FRAMES PER SECOND
entities.description: The rate at which images are updated to ensure motion is perceived as continuous

Perceptual psychology provides guidelines for building better hardware
Perceptual psychology can give clues to the overall idea of presence
Perceptual psychology is the science of how the brain converts sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena
Sensory stimulation is converted by the brain into perceived phenomena
Sense organs are connected to the brain via neural pathways
Video resolution is needed to visualize a virtual object without seeing pixels
Frames per second are necessary to perceive continuous motion in a virtual world
Users may feel nauseated when interacting with certain systems
Different experiences with a system can have different tiring effects on the user
A virtual world is a component or environment within extended reality systems

entities.description: The phenomenon where bodily organs (receptors) are designed to be activated only when a specific type of stimulus arrives.

entities.name: RECEPTOR
entities.description: A sensor within the sense organ that targets particular stimuli.

entities.name: SENSORY ORGAN
entities.description: The hardware of sensing in the human body which contains receptors.

entities.name: PHOTORECEPTORS
entities.description: Receptors in the eyes that get activated by electromagnetic energy in the frequency range of visible light.

entities.name: MECHANORECEPTORS
entities.description: Receptors that sense motion, vibration, or gravitational force.

entities.name: THERMORECEPTORS
entities.description: Receptors involved in the sense of touch to detect changes in temperature.

entities.name: CHEMORECEPTORS
entities.description: Receptors that provide signals based on the chemical composition of matter on the tongue or nasal passage.

entities.name: ELECTROMAGNETIC ENERGY
entities.description: Energy in the form of visible light that activates photoreceptors.

entities.name: VISIBLE LIGHT
entities.description: The frequency range of electromagnetic energy that photoreceptors target.

entities.name: PERCEPTUAL PSYCHOLOGY
entities.description: A field of study required to understand the role of human factors in extended reality systems.

entities.name: PHYSIOLOGY OF SENSES
entities.description: A part of perceptual psychology that deals with the hardware and mechanics of how the body senses the world.
